\chapter*{Pronunciation \& Writing Reference}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{Pronunciation \& Writing Reference}
\markboth{Pronunciation}{Pronunciation}

This is a lookup page, never a prerequisite gate.

\section*{The sounds in Chapter 1}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \textbf{r} in \emph{rām} is a brief tongue-tip tap, not the English bunched or retroflex \emph{r}. Say a quick Spanish-style single \emph{r} if that is familiar.
  \item \textbf{ā} is a steady open vowel held longer than short \emph{a}. The macron in transliteration marks length; Devanagari writes it with \textbf{\mw{ा}} after a consonant.
  \item \textbf{m} and \textbf{s} are close to English \emph{m} and \emph{s}.
\end{itemize}

\section*{The writing rule you need first}

Devanagari consonants carry a built-in short \emph{a}. Thus \textbf{\mw{र}} is \emph{ra} and \textbf{\mw{स}} is \emph{sa}. The right-side mark \textbf{\mw{ा}} changes that vowel to long \emph{ā}: \textbf{\mw{रा}} \emph{rā}, \textbf{\mw{सा}} \emph{sā}. The chapter teaches only those signs and combines them as \textbf{\mw{राम}-\mw{राम} \mw{सा}}.

The lessons ask learners to copy visible forms before they claim a stroke order. Handwriting conventions vary across schools, so a directional stroke sequence will be added only with a specific source. For Marwari-specific Devanagari history and characters, see the \href{https://www.unicode.org/L2/L2010/10475-devanagari-marwari-dda.pdf}{Unicode proposal on Devanagari letters for Marwari}.
